spans.text: QDCVR: An Agent-Operated Platform for Knowledge
Research administrators need to organize document collections and
inspect the evidence behind answers drawn from them. We present
Qdcvr, an agent-operated platform that connects content-guided
knowledge organization with inspectable retrieval. Packaged agent
skills call tool APIs to parse documents, route them among existing
category bases, maintain tags, and read candidate evidence. The
retrieval protocol combines vector recall, a prompted content-gate
self-assessment, additional search and reading, and explicit not-
found reports. Gate scores expose the agent’s judgment; they do not
guarantee semantic correctness. The demonstration lets attendees
follow document placement, inspect retrieved passages and source
references, and examine failure reports. Saved operational traces
cover 50 papers in five bases and 165 stored documents and parts.
A separate ten-question snippet regression passes nine cases, and
three scripted out-of-corpus examples illustrate agent-authored not-
found reports. These operational spot checks provide concrete cases
for examining the workflow, its recorded decisions, and the limits of

category bases, without requiring a new taxonomy. Parsed text,
document parts, and tags support search and reading. Vector recall
feeds a prompted content gate, followed by further search or read-
ing when needed. Gate scores record the agent’s judgment, not a
semantic guarantee. Source references and explicit not-found re-

The organization skill asks the agent to inspect parsed content,
select among existing category bases, and use tools to place and tag
documents. The workflow explicitly checks the resulting parts and
indexing status: successful upload alone does not establish com-
plete tagging and indexing. Administrators retain control over the
bases and permissions. The five-base collection is a demonstration
QDCVR stands for Query-Driven Content-Verified Retrieval. Its
skill rewrites a query, recalls vector candidates across selected
relevance assessment, not guaranteed correctness. The executing
with ranges 0–3, 0–3, and 0–2. A score of at least 6 permits a direct
answer. A score-5 candidate is retained as a partial-evidence back-
stop; candidates scoring at most 4 are discarded. If none scores at
least 6, the librarian inspects base summaries and document meta-
data, searches selectively, and reads new candidates. If no stronger
evidence emerges, the skill permits an explicitly attributed answer
Answers contain search paths, answer, sources, confidence, and
blind spots; evidence is addressable by base, document, part, and
section. If neither strong evidence nor a usable backstop remains,
the skill requests a not-found report with scope, near miss, and
reason. These instructions rely on agent compliance. The supplied
artifacts retain candidate excerpts and answer records; mutable
file-tree metadata is not an append-only per-query audit log.
The demonstration targets research-data administrators and agent
developers. A prepared instance contains 50 papers in five bases.

out-of-corpus probes over 50 papers in five category bases, compris-
ing 165 stored documents and parts. Track A pairs tool-execution
records with saved Qdcvr answers; Track B uses an external agent
with file tools over exported papers; Track C uses dense retrieval
with a 4,000-character context budget. A separate regression using

The three out-of-corpus examples combine script-collected re-
trieval and catalog evidence with predefined agent-authored judg-
ments and templated not-found reports. They illustrate the re-
porting format, not measured autonomous abstention. The census
counts 165 catalog entries but retains 153 document names; it does
not establish exhaustive content inspection. C explicitly abstains in
two of ten saved answers. These records illustrate how insufficient
evidence is reported; non-abstention does not establish correctness.
Gate scores are agent-authored rubric judgments, not independent
correctness assessments. Attendees can inspect the recorded de-
cisions alongside candidate text and source references, including
where the available trace does not fully support an answer.
The tracks use different evidence windows and execution config-
urations. A’s scripted, fixed rewrites include expected-answer terms,
precluding a fair retrieval comparison. B’s file references are self-
reported without retained read events. C loses document metadata
at the logging adapter, a limitation of this reproduction rather than
dense retrieval. Resolved LLM configurations are not archived per
answer, and cache state and parametric knowledge are uncontrolled.
A records retrieval and read times but not answer-authoring time,
so its end-to-end latency is unavailable. These selected traces sup-
port an operational demonstration, not claims of answer accuracy,
Qdcvr links knowledge-base management tools with an agent-
executed workflow for reading evidence, assessing relevance, and
reporting search failure. The demonstration exposes document
placement, source inspection, and not-found behavior. The saved
cases illustrate operation rather than establish general effective-
ness; compliance with the workflow and complete run provenance
